tier_reason: Independent, well-known suite (the-benchmarker/web-frameworks, 7.1k stars): data.json rows tako 2.4 (id 3313) 219,732 / 200,361 / 193,822 req/s and drogon 1.9 (id 55) 177,005 / 178,341 / 171,358 at 64/256/512 match the record; build files (rust/tako/Cargo.toml, rust/Dockerfile, cpp/drogon/config.yaml, cpp/Dockerfile) are public, but the published cpu_name 'M1 Eight-Core Processor' does not identify a CPU model, the C++ compiler version is only implied by the debian:trixie-slim build-essential image, and both servers ran at 57-62% CPU saturation, inside the band the suite's README calls neither valid nor invalid, so not A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: the-benchmarker data.json (updated 2026-10-06): tako 2.4 219,732 / 200,361 / 193,822 req/s at 64 / 256 / 512 connections vs Drogon 1.9.13 177,005 / 178,341 / 171,358 (1.24x / 1.12x / 1.13x, derived from page data); vs agoo-c 0.7 (C) 143,753 / 214,704 / 200,748 (1.53x at 64, 0.93x at 256, 0.97x at 512, derived); vs CWIST 3.9 (C) 186,252 / 166,573 / 162,101 (1.18x / 1.20x / 1.20x, derived). Corroborated in HttpArena (MDA2AV/HttpArena site/data/results/tako.json and drogon.json, Threadripper PRO 3995WX): baseline-4096 3,258,564 vs Drogon 2,022,710 (1.61x), limited-conn-4096 2,474,910 vs 1,694,883 (1.46x), pipelined-4096 22,082,892 vs 7,801,404 (2.83x), json-comp-4096 212,739 vs 127,466 (1.67x), json-tls-4096 904,303 vs 253,055 (3.57x), latency-500k-8cpu 470,285 vs 374,962 (1.25x), 8gbit-512 48,998 vs 49,360 (0.99x), all derived from page data.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: the-benchmarker: tako built in rust:1.98-slim with cargo build --release, Cargo.toml release profile opt-level 3, lto = true, codegen-units = 1, panic = abort (the Dockerfile repeats lto/panic/codegen-units via --config), tako-rs 2.4 with feature per-thread, no target-cpu. Drogon v1.9.13 built in debian:trixie-slim with build-essential (GCC 14 from Debian trixie, inferred from the image) via cmake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=release (CMake's Release flags -O3 -DNDEBUG), C++17, no LTO, no -march; config.json threads_num 0 (one IO thread per core). HttpArena: tako built in rust:1.99-trixie with RUSTFLAGS='-C target-cpu=native', lto = 'fat', codegen-units = 1; Drogon built from drogonframework/drogon:latest with CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release (no -march=native, compiler version not stated) and run with LD_PRELOAD jemalloc.
corrections.hardware: the-benchmarker data.json hardware field: cpu_name 'M1 Eight-Core Processor' (does not name a recognisable CPU model), 16 logical CPUs, 7,733,008 kB RAM, Linux 7.2.7-200.fc44.x86_64; per-run server_cpu_cores / server_cpu_saturation imply about 4 CPUs allotted to each server container (derived from page data). HttpArena current.json: AMD Ryzen Threadripper PRO 3995WX (64 cores, 128 threads), 251 GiB, Ubuntu 24.04.4, kernel 6.17.0-22, governor performance.
corrections.stars_or_usage: 163 stars; tako-rs crate 5,186 downloads (crates.io API, 2026-10-12; latest 2.4.1)
corrections.caveats: The suite win is architectural (thread-per-core runtime with SO_REUSEPORT listeners), not a Rust language effect, and margins are small (1.12-1.24x over Drogon; agoo-c (C) beats tako at 256 and 512 connections). The README's own benchmark compares only against Actix Web, ntex and Axum on a 24 vCPU EPYC 9655P container (not C or C++). the-benchmarker weaknesses: one published snapshot (data.json updated 2026-10-06, no repeat spread); the suite README says above 75% server CPU saturation the number is the framework's and below 50% it is not, and tako (56-57%) and Drogon (62-63%) both sit in the band between; the 57 of the 60 fastest rows at 256 connections that carry a saturation value range 49-69% (suite median 71%), so the fastest servers may be generator-bound; the README describes the current method as zrk --closed keep-alive (saturation fields exist only in that method, so this snapshot is probably that revision, inferred) but an older paragraph still describes oha with keep-alive disabled; three trivial routes with near-empty bodies. Flags differ: Rust side uses LTO and codegen-units 1, Drogon has no LTO; in HttpArena the Rust side is built with target-cpu=native and Drogon generically, and the HttpArena tako entry is maintained by the tako author (meta.json maintainers dancixx). HttpArena does not generalise the win to nginx: level on baseline-4096 (3,258,564 vs nginx 3,284,513, 0.99x) and far behind on HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 (baseline-h2-256 741,740 vs 3,414,750; baseline-h3-64 534,205 vs 4,849,624) and static TLS (142,858 vs 720,869). nginx, h2o and lithium are not rows in the-benchmarker; same-table losers to Drogon at 256 connections include Crystal toro, Go fasthttp and C# aspnet-minimal-api.

notes: Numbers verified in the-benchmarker data.json and corroborated by HttpArena, where tako also beats Drogon by 1.25-3.57x on most shared tests (8gbit tie), though HttpArena builds tako with target-cpu=native against a generic Drogon build. Shortcomings: architectural not language-level win, 1.12-1.24x margins, saturation in the suite's grey zone, unidentifiable CPU string, LTO/native-flag asymmetry, loses to agoo-c (C) at 256/512 and to nginx on HTTP/2, HTTP/3 and static TLS in HttpArena.

tier_reason: First-party wrk numbers in documentation/readme/benchmarks.rst match the record (kawipiko 106,698.89 / 100,296.65 / 95,628.34 / 53,548.52 vs NGinx 79,816.08 / 78,211.46 / 75,970.82 / 43,909.67; tiles 238,499.86 vs 188,255.32); kawipiko's Go version and flags and NGinx's version and build are not stated, so C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Hello World over loopback, 2 server threads, 2 wrk threads: kawipiko 106,698.89 / 100,296.65 / 95,628.34 / 53,548.52 req/s at 512 / 2048 / 4096 / 16384 connections (section 'Last updated in August 2018') vs NGinx 79,816.08 / 78,211.46 / 75,970.82 / 43,909.67 (section 'Last updated in August 2019'), 1.34x / 1.28x / 1.26x / 1.22x (derived from page data, pairing the two separately dated sections). OpenStreetMap tile run (one section, August 2019, i7 4770, 8 threads, 16384 connections, 2 minutes): kawipiko --archive-inmem 238,499.86 req/s, --archive-mmap 237,239.35, 8 processes mmap 248,266.83 vs NGinx 8 workers 188,255.32 (1.27x / 1.26x / 1.32x, derived); the author states ~25% more requests/s, ~29% lower average latency, ~40% lower p90 latency, ~25% less CPU per request, while NGinx used the least RAM and kawipiko about 1 GiB. The summary (December 2021) calls kawipiko 'at least on-par with NGinx'.
corrections.caveats: First-party, measured on 2013-era CPUs (i7 3667U laptop, i7 4770 desktop) with an older kawipiko version (the author says the current one is at least 10% more efficient). The Hello World kawipiko rows (August 2018) and NGinx rows (August 2019) are in separately dated sections, so the 1.22-1.34x ratios compare runs a year apart; only the tile run is a same-session comparison. kawipiko was requested at '/' and NGinx at '/index.txt' (the author chose the path he says favours NGinx). NGinx is a distribution package with an author-tuned config (examples/nginx); kawipiko ran with --archive-inmem, --security-headers-disable and --timeout-disable (the author says timeouts cost 10-15%). wrk reports socket errors for kawipiko at every row from 512 connections (timeouts 86 / 4,449 / 2,288 at 2048 / 4096 / 16384, versus NGinx 11 / 187 / 1,121) and in both tile runs (kawipiko 7,032 timeouts, NGinx 16,833). The tile CDB was deduplicated to ~100k of ~250k files, and the wrk command shown targets a single URL, so how the tile list was driven is not shown. The author says kawipiko over HTTP/2 is about 6x slower than its own HTTPS over HTTP/1, where NGinx is not. The author says the real advantage is deployment simplicity. The win comes from the CDB in-memory design on fasthttp, not from Go versus C codegen.

notes: Numbers match benchmarks.rst; tier C stands (first-party, Go and NGinx builds unstated). Shortcomings: the Hello World ratio pairs kawipiko rows from August 2018 with NGinx rows from August 2019 (cross-run), only the 1.27x tile run is same-session; timeouts and security headers disabled for kawipiko; more wrk timeouts for kawipiko than NGinx at 4096 connections; 2013-era CPUs, old version; the author calls it 'at least on-par'.

tier_reason: First-party numbers in the README and bench/BENCHMARK_RESULTS.md match the record (June 189,810 vs nginx 153,484; August 323,035 vs 282,032 and HAProxy 266,603); the August script bench/haproxy_baseline.sh is public but needs a missing bench_config.yml and a vendored HAProxy not in the repo, and nginx's version and build flags are not stated, so C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: June run (bench/BENCHMARK_RESULTS.md, 2026-06-27, median of 3 after warmup, proxies pinned to cores 2-3 with 2 workers each): rproxy 189,810.00 req/s (557 us) vs nginx reverse proxy 153,484.52 (662 us) = 1.24x; rproxy before its hot-path optimisation 135,700.79 (0.88x); backend ceiling 362,163.20. August run (README, measured 2026-08-16 with bench/haproxy_baseline.sh, labelled median of 3 but the script keeps the best of 3): rproxy 323,035 (352 us) vs nginx reverse proxy 282,032 (400 us) = 1.15x and HAProxy 2.8.5 266,603 (395 us) = 1.21x; ceiling 632,175. rproxy with TLS 134,168 req/s (no TLS comparison against nginx).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Cargo release profile: lto = 'fat', codegen-units = 1, panic = 'abort', opt-level = 3, debug = true; monoio 0.2.4 with io_uring. nginx version and build flags not stated (installed from the system, per the script's 'command -v nginx'); HAProxy 2.8.5 vendored build, flags not stated.
corrections.hardware: 12th Gen Intel Core i5-12450H, 12 logical cores; June run: wrk on cores 4-7, backend nginx on cores 0-1, proxy on cores 2-3. The August script does no pinning: backend nginx and the nginx proxy each run worker_processes 4, HAProxy and rproxy use their defaults, all on the same box.
corrections.caveats: First-party; both runs (2026-06-27 and 2026-08-16) predate the repo's first public commit (2026-08-18), so the measured revisions are not in public history. The August three-proxy run's script (bench/haproxy_baseline.sh) labels its result 'median-of-3' but keeps the best of 3 runs, pins no cores, gives the nginx proxy worker_processes 4 and reads rproxy's worker count from bench_config.yml, which is not in the repo, so the equal-core claim holds only for the June run; that also explains the ceiling jump from 362k (2 pinned backend cores) to 632k (4 unpinned workers). The June nginx proxy config is not published and its upstream keep-alive is not stated (bench/nginx_proxy.conf in the repo listens on 8081 and proxies to 8081, so it is not the config used). The README is internally inconsistent about HAProxy: it shows a measured HAProxy row and then says 'HAProxy was not measured on the current rig' and no HAProxy comparison is claimed. Tiny 2-byte keep-alive body, same box, no TLS comparison; larger bodies, no keep-alive or TLS may differ. No LICENSE file, so reference. 0 stars, 2 commits. The README positions rproxy as a filter behind nginx, not a replacement. The win is architectural (prefork thread-per-core monoio workers on io_uring, coalesced head+body writes), not a Rust language effect.

notes: Numbers match README and bench/BENCHMARK_RESULTS.md; tier C stands. Shortcomings: haproxy_baseline.sh reports best-of-3 labelled median and pins nothing, needs a bench_config.yml absent from the repo; June nginx config unpublished (repo copy is a self-loop); measured code predates public history; contradictory HAProxy statements; 2-byte keep-alive body only; no licence; 0 stars.
